meta.audience: All the people of Zarahemla, assembled by families at the temple
meta.location: The temple in the land of Zarahemla

world_behind.title: A festival assembly, by families, in tents
world_behind.text: They bring firstlings for burnt offerings, camp around the temple by household, and pitch every tent with its door toward the sanctuary. Israel's wilderness camp was arranged around the tabernacle by family, and the autumn festival was kept in booths. Every element here belongs to that pattern.

world_behind.title: The door faces the sanctuary
world_behind.text: Verse 6 gives a practical reason (they could hear from inside their tents), but the arrangement also puts every household oriented toward one point. Whether the record means it as architecture or as posture, it describes both.

world_behind.title: A tower, and a published text
world_behind.text: Benjamin builds a platform to be heard, and when that fails he has the words written and distributed to those out of earshot. Ezra stood on a wooden pulpit to read the law to an assembly; this adds publication. The sermon the reader has is the distributed copy.

world_behind.title: A king who worked and took no taxes
world_behind.text: Verse 14 has Benjamin laboring with his own hands so the people would not be laden. In the ancient world a king's revenue was normally the point of the office. The record presents the refusal as remarkable and expects the audience to agree.

world_behind.title: "Unprofitable servants," from Luke's parable
world_behind.text: Verse 21 reaches the same conclusion as Luke 17:10: a servant who has done all that was commanded is still unprofitable. Benjamin arrives at it by a different route, counting breath as lent moment by moment.

world_behind.title: The Spirit withdrawn rather than sent away
world_behind.text: Verse 36 says a man who transgresses withdraws himself from the Spirit. The grammar puts the motion on the man. Verse 37 completes it: the Lord has no place in him, because he does not dwell in unholy temples. That is Stephen's line about temples made with hands, turned inward.

words.text: To treat as of little consequence, and in the King James Bible the sense is dismissive handling rather than joking. Benjamin says he did not summon them to trifle with his words. The warning is issued before the sermon begins and it is about attention, not about belief.

Weaknesses of body or mind. Benjamin claims them for himself in the same sentence in which he reports being chosen, consecrated, and preserved. The word does the work of the whole passage: the office is real and the man in it is ordinary.

The verb means to permit. Treated at 2 Nephi 6:11. Benjamin says "Neither have I suffered that ye should be confined in dungeons" (v. 13), and the same word runs through the passage in both directions: the Lord suffered him to be a ruler, suffered him to spend his days in service, and at the last suffered him to speak. What he grants or withholds among his people he holds only because it was granted to him first. A modern reader hears pain in the word. None of these sentences is about pain.

cites.quote: Neither have I suffered that ye should be confined in dungeons

spans.text: Neither have I suffered that ye should be confined in dungeons

words.text: An archaic verb meaning to choose or to desire. To list to obey is to be inclined to. Used three times of obedience to the evil spirit, it makes the relationship voluntary. Nothing in Benjamin's account of damnation happens to a man who did not want it.

To draw back from something, bodily. The King James Bible never uses the verb this way; its one appearance there is a sinew that shrank at Peniel. Here it names what guilt does in God's presence: justice wakes the man to a sense of his own guilt, "which doth cause him to shrink from the presence of the Lord" (v. 38). Everything else in the verse is legal wording, demands and claims and a sentence. The one word for what actually happens to the man is a movement away.

cites.quote: which doth cause him to shrink from the presence of the Lord

spans.text: which doth cause him to shrink from the presence of the Lord

words.text: A judicial sentence. The King James sense is the verdict handed down. The word does not name an assigned destiny. Benjamin says mercy has no claim on such a man and his final doom is never-ending torment. The legal wording is deliberate: the previous verse has justice making demands.

phrases.term: Every man having his tent with the door thereof towards the temple
phrases.text: A whole nation's households oriented toward one building. The stated reason is acoustic and the effect is architectural. Nothing in the verse explains why every door rather than most, and the detail is recorded with a precision that suggests an eyewitness.

phrases.term: Open your ears that ye may hear, and your hearts that ye may understand
phrases.text: Three organs, three verbs, in ascending order: ears to hear, hearts to understand, minds for the mysteries to be unfolded. Benjamin assigns the audience work before he says anything, and the distribution of tasks across ears, heart, and mind is the sermon's theory of how listening happens.

phrases.term: I of myself am more than a mortal man
phrases.text: The denial is placed before any teaching. Benjamin is dismantling his own authority as a first move, and the phrasing "of myself" leaves room for what he does claim later. Kings in the ancient Near East were routinely more than mortal by definition.

phrases.term: I might serve you, and that ye should not be laden with taxes
phrases.text: The sentence names the two things a king normally does not do: manual labor and forgoing revenue. Benjamin offers the people as witnesses in the same breath, so the audience can check it. His claim is that the office cost him.

phrases.term: When ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God
phrases.text: The chapter's most quoted sentence, and the word carrying it is "only." Benjamin is not saying service of others resembles service of God or pleases him; he is saying there is no third category. The argument starts with his own case, a king serving and therefore serving God, and runs outward to everyone listening.

phrases.term: By lending you breath, that ye may live and move
phrases.text: Breath as a loan, and the tense is continuous. The preserving is from day to day, the supporting from one moment to another. Paul told the Athenians that in him we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28); Benjamin turns the same thought into an account that can never be settled because the borrowing has not stopped. The same verse states the conclusion of that arithmetic: "yet ye would be unprofitable servants" (v. 21). Serve with your whole soul and the balance is still against you, since the service is performed with borrowed breath. Luke's parable reaches the same phrase from duty (Luke 17:10); Benjamin reaches it from debt, and the two meet exactly.

cites.quote: yet ye would be unprofitable servants

spans.text: yet ye would be unprofitable servants

phrases.term: He doth immediately bless you; and therefore he hath paid you
phrases.text: The most startling sentence in the address. Obedience is compensated on the spot. No credit ever accrues. Benjamin closes the loop deliberately: you are indebted, you obey, you are paid, you are indebted again. Then he asks what there is to boast of.

phrases.term: Ye cannot say that ye are even as much as the dust of the earth
phrases.text: The dust obeys and belongs to its maker; the audience does neither reliably. It is a statement about ownership. Even the material they were made from is somebody else's. Verse 26 has Benjamin including himself, so worthlessness is not the point.

phrases.term: That I might rid my garments of your blood
phrases.text: Jacob said sins; Benjamin says blood; Jacob's own first chapter said blood too. The figure is fixed across five hundred years and three speakers, and each one specifies the stain himself. Benjamin's reason is that he wants to go down to his grave in peace.

phrases.term: Ye do withdraw yourselves from the Spirit of the Lord
phrases.text: The subject of the verb is the person. Nothing is taken away; someone steps back. Benjamin's account of losing the Spirit assigns the motion entirely to the one who loses it, and the next verse explains the result.

phrases.term: The Lord has no place in him, for he dwelleth not in unholy temples
phrases.text: The body as a building, and the reason given for the absence is a matter of what God does rather than of what he refuses. Stephen said the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands; Benjamin applies the same principle to a person, and the record will use the phrase three more times.

phrases.term: The blessed and happy state of those that keep the commandments of God
phrases.text: The address ends on the alternative. Two verses of torment are followed by one of happiness, temporal and spiritual, and a doubled imperative to remember. The proportion is deliberate and the last word is that the Lord has spoken it.

verses.label: v. 5–6
verses.title: Tents pointed at the temple
verses.text: The arrangement is described with a detail no summary requires: "they pitched their tents round about, every man according to his family," and then "every man having his tent with the door thereof towards the temple, that thereby they might remain in their tents and hear the words which king Benjamin should speak unto them." The orientation is given a purpose in the same sentence. Families stay housed and still face the speaker, which is a solution to the same acoustic problem the tower addresses.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: A king declining the status of his office
verses.text: The address opens by ruling out two readings of the summons: "I have not commanded you to come up hither that ye should fear me, or that ye should think that I of myself am more than a mortal man." Verse 11 states the positive claim in the plainest terms available, "I am like as yourselves, subject to all manner of infirmities in body and mind," and only then mentions the office, "yet I have been chosen by this people, and consecrated by my father."

verses.label: v. 12–14
verses.title: A reign described entirely by what did not happen
verses.text: The record gives the king's account of his own rule as a list of negatives: he has "not sought gold nor silver nor any manner of riches of you"; "Neither have I suffered that ye should be confined in dungeons, nor that ye should make slaves one of another, nor that ye should murder, or plunder, or steal"; and "I, myself, have labored with mine own hands that I might serve you, and that ye should not be laden with taxes." Six things not done and one thing done, and the one is manual work.

verses.label: v. 15–16
verses.title: A disclaimer attached to the disclaimer
verses.text: Having listed his record, the record has the speaker deny two possible motives for listing it: "I have not done these things that I might boast, neither do I tell these things that thereby I might accuse you." Verse 16 goes over the same ground a second time, "because I said unto you that I had spent my days in your service, I do not desire to boast, for I have only been in the service of God." Two verses are spent on why the previous three verses were spoken, and the reason finally given in verse 17 is instruction, "that ye may learn wisdom."

verses.label: v. 20–24
verses.title: An accounting argument, with the steps numbered
verses.text: The record puts the case as a ledger that cannot balance: "if you should render all the thanks and praise which your whole soul has power to possess... yet ye would be unprofitable servants." That phrase stands at Luke 17:10 in the same construction. Verses 23 and 24 then set out the reckoning in order, "in the first place, he hath created you, and granted unto you your lives, for which ye are indebted unto him. And secondly, he doth require that ye should do as he hath commanded you; for which if ye do, he doth immediately bless you." Each payment creates a new debt, and the record numbers the two steps so the loop is visible.

verses.label: v. 25–26
verses.title: The dust comparison, turned on the speaker
verses.text: The question is asked and answered in the same verse: "can ye say aught of yourselves? I answer you, Nay. Ye cannot say that ye are even as much as the dust of the earth." Verse 26 then applies the same measure to the man on the tower: "I, even I, whom ye call your king, am no better than ye yourselves are; for I am also of the dust." The argument would work without the second verse. The record includes it, and puts the king inside the class he has just described.

chapter.title: The king spends his authority dismantling itself
chapter.text: Before any doctrine, Benjamin denies being more than mortal, claims infirmities, lists what he did not take, and calls his reign service. Everything he says afterward about indebtedness is credible because he has already applied it to himself, out loud, in front of witnesses he names.

chapter.title: Service is collapsed into a single category
chapter.text: Verse 17 does not compare service of others to service of God; it identifies them. The word "only" removes the middle term. It is the most consequential sentence in the address and it is derived from Benjamin's own biography rather than from scripture.

chapter.title: The debt can never be reduced, by design
chapter.text: Creation puts you in debt; obedience is paid immediately; therefore nothing accumulates on your side. Benjamin builds a closed system, and the reason boasting is unavailable inside it is structural.

chapter.title: Losing the Spirit is described as an act of the person
chapter.text: Verse 36 has the man withdrawing himself; verse 37 explains that God's absence follows from what God is. Nothing in the passage has the Spirit departing in anger. The account is mechanical about a subject usually handled as an emotional one.

chapter.title: The physical arrangements get as much care as the theology
chapter.text: Five logistical facts stand in four verses. Families camp "every man according to his family... from the eldest down to the youngest" at verse 5. Every tent door faces the temple at verse 6. A tower is built because "the multitude being so great that king Benjamin could not teach them all within the walls of the temple" at verse 7. Even the tower fails, so "he caused that the words which he spake should be written and sent forth among those that were not under the sound of his voice" at verse 8. An abridgment covering a thousand years keeps the seating plan, and Mosiah 6:1 depends on the reader remembering that a written text existed.

chapter.title: The address is a farewell that installs a successor mid-sermon
chapter.text: Verse 30 announces Mosiah as king inside a discourse on service and debt. The political act is embedded in the religious one, and the people are asked to obey the son on the same terms they obeyed the father.

chapter.title: Justice and mercy are given a courtroom
chapter.text: Demands, claims, wages, a doom, a witness, a blameless defendant. Verses 27 through 39 run almost entirely on legal vocabulary, and the man using it is the nation's judge describing his own approaching trial.

applications.title: Point the door
applications.text: Every household faced the same direction before a word was spoken. Ask what your home is physically and practically oriented toward, and whether that matches what you would say it is oriented toward.

applications.title: Assign yourself the listening work
applications.text: Ears, heart, mind: Benjamin gives the audience three jobs before he starts. Before your next meeting, lesson, or difficult conversation, decide specifically what you are opening.

applications.title: Serve where it costs you
applications.text: Benjamin's credibility comes from having declined the benefits of his office. Find one place where you could take something you are entitled to, and decline it quietly.

applications.title: Stop sorting service into sacred and ordinary
applications.text: The verse removes the category. Take the most mundane thing you will do for someone this week and treat it as the whole of what it is.

applications.title: Run the debt honestly
applications.text: Count what you have been given against what you have returned, including the breath you are using to count. The point is not guilt; it is the end of boasting.

applications.title: Notice who is doing the withdrawing
applications.text: When God seems distant, Benjamin's grammar puts the motion on you. Ask what you have stepped back from before concluding that something was taken.

applications.title: Weigh the two states
applications.text: He asks old men, young men, and children to consider both outcomes side by side. Do that literally, writing the two columns, rather than only attending to the one that frightens you.

questions.text: Do I come to instruction expecting to work, or expecting to be entertained?
What have I taken from a position that I could have gone without?
Whose service today am I filing under "not really spiritual"?
If breath is lent by the moment, what does that change about how I hold anything else?
What am I quietly keeping a ledger of, expecting it to count for something?
Where have I withdrawn, and would I have described it that way?
Do I actually believe the happy state is better, or only that the other one is worse?
